reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett / ATS-IDSA NTM guidance
clinicalPearls: A slow-growing scotochromogen (producing yellow-orange pigment even in the dark) named for its historical role in scrofula
Was a classic cause of cervical lymphadenitis in young children before Mycobacterium avium complex became the predominant cause
Acquired from the environment, including water, soil, and formerly raw dairy products, typically entering through the mouth and pharynx
Presents in a child of one to five years as a unilateral, firm, painless, enlarging neck node with little systemic upset
Untreated nodes may soften, discolour the overlying skin, and drain through a chronic sinus
Complete surgical excision of the affected node is the treatment of choice and is usually curative
Antimicrobial therapy is adjunctive, reserved for incomplete excision, recurrence, or extensive disease, and incision and drainage should be avoided because it promotes sinus formation
reference.pathophysiology: Mycobacterium scrofulaceum is a slow-growing scotochromogenic environmental mycobacterium. In young children it is thought to enter through the oropharyngeal mucosa and spread to draining cervical and submandibular lymph nodes, where a granulomatous response with caseation develops. The relatively contained immune response accounts for the localised, minimally symptomatic adenitis; progressive necrosis can liquefy and track to the skin, producing discolouration, fluctuance, and a chronically discharging sinus. In older or immunocompromised patients pulmonary and disseminated disease occur uncommonly.
additionalDifferentials: Branchial cleft cyst or other congenital neck swelling
additionalInvestigations: Excisional lymph-node biopsy for histology and mycobacterial culture
Mycobacterial culture with recognition of scotochromogenic pigment
Tuberculin skin test and interferon-gamma release assay to help exclude tuberculosis
Ultrasound of the neck to define the extent of nodal disease
Assessment of immune status in atypical, extensive, or recurrent disease
redFlags: Involvement near the facial nerve where surgery risks nerve injury
Features suggesting tuberculosis requiring exclusion and contact tracing
Extensive, bilateral, or recurrent disease suggesting immunodeficiency
Rapidly enlarging or systemically symptomatic swelling suggesting malignancy
reference.prognosis: Childhood cervical lymphadenitis has an excellent prognosis after complete surgical excision, which is generally curative. Incomplete excision or inappropriate incision and drainage can lead to chronic sinuses and prolonged healing. Pulmonary and disseminated disease are uncommon and carry a more guarded outlook.
pitfalls: Performing incision and drainage, which promotes a chronic discharging sinus
Failing to exclude tuberculosis before attributing adenitis to nontuberculous mycobacteria
Delaying diagnosis by not sending tissue for mycobacterial culture and molecular testing
Risking facial-nerve injury during excision of periparotid nodes
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
